explanations.explanation: That's exactly the reason the verse gives: “…Do not be arrogant, for the LORD has spoken.” (Jeremiah 13:15) When God has spoken, a big head has nowhere to stand. My chef's hat is tall enough already, and even I tip it down a little.

The verse never mentions enemies watching. The reason it gives is right there in the same sentence: “…Do not be arrogant, for the LORD has spoken.” Worrying about who's watching is how a baker ends up sneaking dough with the lights off, and that's a different problem.

explanations.answer: Because the king has commanded it
explanations.explanation: No king gives an order in this verse. The reason is “…Do not be arrogant, for the LORD has spoken.” (Jeremiah 13:15) The king doesn't show up until verse 18, and there he's the one being told something.

True. The verse says, “…You wait for light, but He turns it into deep gloom and thick darkness.” (Jeremiah 13:16) Waiting on light and getting thicker dark is a heavy picture. I spent years in a dark junk drawer, so I know how long waiting for light can feel.

It's actually true. Jeremiah 13:16 says, “…You wait for light, but He turns it into deep gloom and thick darkness.” The verse before it asks them to give glory to the LORD their God before He brings that darkness. So the card repeats the verse just as it's written.

explanations.answer: Weep in secret because of their pride
explanations.explanation: That's it. The verse says, “But if you do not listen, I will weep in secret because of your pride.” (Jeremiah 13:17) I think this is where you see how much Jeremiah, God's prophet, cares. He isn't gloating, he's crying where nobody can see.

explanations.answer: Leave Jerusalem and never come back
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the verse says he'll leave. What he says is, “But if you do not listen, I will weep in secret because of your pride.” (Jeremiah 13:17) Weeping in secret is a very different thing from walking out the door.

explanations.answer: Stop bringing them the LORD’s word
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't say he'll stop speaking. It says he will “weep in secret because of your pride.” (Jeremiah 13:17) I think this one hurts, because it shows a prophet who cares about the people he's warning.

explanations.answer: The LORD’s flock has been taken captive
explanations.explanation: Right. Jeremiah says, “My eyes will overflow with tears, because the LORD’s flock has been taken captive.” (Jeremiah 13:17) The flock means the LORD's people, taken away. That's a heavy part, and the tears are real.

explanations.answer: The temple has been torn to the ground
explanations.explanation: The temple isn't mentioned in this verse. The reason for the tears is “…because the LORD’s flock has been taken captive.” (Jeremiah 13:17) It's about people, not a building. I think that's what makes it hurt.

explanations.answer: The king has turned the city against him
explanations.explanation: The verse says nothing about the king turning on Jeremiah, God's prophet. The tears come “because the LORD’s flock has been taken captive.” (Jeremiah 13:17) His grief is for the people, not for himself.

Yes, lowly. The king and the queen mother are told, “Take a lowly seat, for your glorious crowns have fallen from your heads.” (Jeremiah 13:18) The queen mother is the king's mother. I've been moved from the counter to the back of a drawer, so I know what a lowly seat feels like.

Royal sounds right for a king, but the text says lowly. The seat they're told to take is “a lowly seat,” because their “glorious crowns have fallen from your heads.” (Jeremiah 13:18) The royal part is exactly what they're losing.

Golden would fit a crown, but not this seat. The verse says, “Take a lowly seat, for your glorious crowns have fallen from your heads.” (Jeremiah 13:18) The gold has fallen and the seat is the humble kind. Nobody gets a gold seat when the crown has fallen off.

The text goes much further than a few towns. It says, “All Judah has been carried into exile, wholly taken captive.” (Jeremiah 13:19) That's the whole land, not just a few places. The cities of the Negev are shut tight, and no one can open them.

That's right, it's false. Jeremiah 13:19 says, “All Judah has been carried into exile, wholly taken captive.” Not a few towns, friend. All of Judah, wholly taken. The word doing the work there is “wholly.”

North it is. The message says, “Lift up your eyes and see those coming from the north.” (Jeremiah 13:20) It's a call to look up and see them coming. The verse names a direction and nothing more, so I'll leave it there.

South shows up in verse 19, where the cities of the Negev are shut tight. But the ones coming in verse 20 are “coming from the north.” (Jeremiah 13:20) Same passage, different direction. Easy to mix up when the verses sit side by side.

The text doesn't send anyone from the east. It says, “Lift up your eyes and see those coming from the north.” (Jeremiah 13:20) The direction is stated plainly. A baker could check the oven twice and still not turn it around.

Labor is right. The verse asks, “Will not pangs of anguish grip you, as they do a woman in labor?” (Jeremiah 13:21) It's a picture of pain that grabs hold and won't let go. It shows how deep the anguish will be.
Court doesn't fit here. The verse says the anguish grips them “as they do a woman in labor.” (Jeremiah 13:21) It's a picture of sudden, gripping pain, not a trial.
Battle is a fair guess, but the verse says labor. It asks, “Will not pangs of anguish grip you, as they do a woman in labor?” (Jeremiah 13:21) The comparison is pain that grips and won't let go.

That's not what the text says. The answer to “Why has this happened to me?” is “…because of the magnitude of your iniquity…” (Jeremiah 13:22) Their enemies being too strong isn't the reason given. The reason is about their own iniquity.

False is right. The text answers, “It is because of the magnitude of your iniquity that your skirts have been stripped off and your body has been exposed.” (Jeremiah 13:22) It doesn't say anything about enemies being too strong. It's a straight answer to a question they hadn't even asked yet.

explanations.answer: They can’t do good when they’re used to evil
explanations.explanation: That's the point. The verse says, “Neither are you able to do good—you who are accustomed to doing evil.” (Jeremiah 13:23) Ask a leopard to swap spots and you get a very patient look and no change. The question says that doing evil has become their habit.

explanations.answer: They will change once the trouble comes
explanations.explanation: The verse says the opposite. After the question about the Ethiopian and the leopard, it says, “Neither are you able to do good—you who are accustomed to doing evil.” (Jeremiah 13:23) Nothing in it says the trouble will change them.

explanations.answer: They are no worse than the other nations
explanations.explanation: The verse never compares them to other nations. It says, “Neither are you able to do good—you who are accustomed to doing evil.” (Jeremiah 13:23) The question about skin and spots is about them and their habit of evil. It's not a ranking.

Forgotten is right. The LORD says this is their lot “because you have forgotten Me and trusted in falsehood.” (Jeremiah 13:25) Forgetting Him and trusting falsehood go together in that sentence. It's a sad pair of words.
Honored is the opposite of what the verse says. The LORD says this is their lot “because you have forgotten Me and trusted in falsehood.” (Jeremiah 13:25) The text doesn't say they honored Him.

Obeyed doesn't fit this verse. It says, “…because you have forgotten Me and trusted in falsehood.” (Jeremiah 13:25) The text says they forgot Him, not that they obeyed Him. The portion measured out to them comes with that reason attached.

True. The LORD says, “I have seen your detestable acts.” (Jeremiah 13:27) This is one of the heavy parts of the passage, and I won't make light of it. The LORD names what He has seen, and then He calls out, “Woe to you, O Jerusalem!”
It's true, friend. The LORD says, “…I have seen your detestable acts.” (Jeremiah 13:27) This is a heavy part, so I'll just say it plainly. He has seen, and He says so right there in the verse.

explanations.answer: How long it will remain unclean
explanations.explanation: That's the closing question. The LORD says, “Woe to you, O Jerusalem! How long will you remain unclean?” (Jeremiah 13:27) It's a question left hanging at the end of the passage. The text doesn't answer it here.

explanations.answer: Why it went back to Egypt
explanations.explanation: Egypt doesn't come up in this verse. After “Woe to you, O Jerusalem!” the LORD asks, “How long will you remain unclean?” (Jeremiah 13:27) The question is about staying unclean, not about going anywhere.
Nothing in this verse mentions walls or rebuilding. After “Woe to you, O Jerusalem!” the LORD asks, “How long will you remain unclean?” (Jeremiah 13:27) That's the question on the table at the end.
